name: GDP by the Expenditure Approach
description: Adds consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).
notes: Transfer payments are not part of G.

name: Taylor Rule Policy Rate
description: Suggests a central-bank policy rate from inflation and the output gap (Taylor 1993): r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5 × gap.
notes: Here 5.5 %. Central banks use it as a benchmark, not a mechanical rule.

name: Output Gap
description: Gives how far actual output is above (positive) or below (negative) its potential.
notes: Negative gaps mean slack and downward pressure on inflation.

name: Public Debt Dynamics
description: Gives next year's debt-to-GDP ratio from the interest rate, growth and the primary balance.
notes: When r < g the ratio can fall even with small primary deficits.

name: Primary Balance that Stabilises Debt
description: Gives the primary surplus (as a share of GDP) that keeps the debt ratio constant.
notes: Negative means a primary deficit is compatible with a stable ratio.

name: Misery Index
description: Adds the unemployment rate and the inflation rate (Okun).
notes: A rough gauge of economic discomfort.

name: Harrod–Domar Growth Rate
description: Gives the growth rate an economy can sustain from its saving rate and capital–output ratio.
notes: A simple post-war model, now mostly of historical interest.

name: Relative Purchasing Power Parity
description: Predicts next year's exchange rate from the inflation differential.
notes: Holds poorly in the short run but reasonably over many years.

name: Growth Accounting (Solow Residual)
description: Gives total factor productivity growth: output growth not explained by more capital and labour.
notes: Here 0.95 % a year.

name: Gini Coefficient from Incomes
expression: sum(i, 1, len(x), sum(j, 1, len(x), abs(at(x, i) - at(x, j)))) / (2 * len(x)^2 * mean(x))
description: Computes the Gini coefficient from individual incomes as the mean absolute difference over twice the mean.
notes: 0 is perfect equality, 1 maximal inequality. Country values range roughly from 0.25 to 0.6.

name: Theil Index
description: Measures inequality with Theil's entropy index T = mean((xᵢ/μ) ln(xᵢ/μ)).
notes: Can be split into within-group and between-group parts.

name: Atkinson Inequality Index
description: Gives the share of total income society would give up for perfect equality, for inequality aversion ε (Atkinson 1970).
notes: Higher ε puts more weight on the lowest incomes.

name: Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (Any Number of Firms)
description: Adds the squared market shares of all firms (in percent). Competition authorities use it to screen mergers.
notes: Below 1500 unconcentrated, above 2500 highly concentrated (US guidelines).

name: Concentration Ratio CR4
description: Adds the market shares of the four largest firms.
notes: Above about 60 % is usually called an oligopoly.

name: Laspeyres Price Index
description: Prices a fixed basket of base-period quantities at current and base prices; the method behind most consumer price indices.
notes: Tends to overstate inflation because it ignores substitution.

name: Paasche Price Index
description: Weights prices by current-period quantities.
notes: Tends to understate inflation; GDP deflators are Paasche-type.

name: Fisher Ideal Price Index
expression: sqrt(dot(p1, q0) / dot(p0, q0) * dot(p1, q1) / dot(p0, q1)) * 100
description: Takes the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices; it passes the time- and factor-reversal tests.
notes: Used for US GDP and many chained indices.

name: Real GDP Growth from Nominal Growth and Inflation
description: Removes price growth from nominal GDP growth to give real growth.
notes: Approximately gn − inflation for small rates.

name: Sacrifice Ratio
description: Gives the percentage of a year's output lost for each point of disinflation.
notes: Estimates for advanced economies are typically 1–3.

name: Employment-to-Population Ratio
description: Gives the share of the working-age population that has a job.
notes: Not affected by people giving up looking for work, unlike the unemployment rate.
